newsitem.title: USA: Stock replacing retirement plans for directors - survey.
newsitem.headline: Stock replacing retirement plans for directors - survey.

text.p: More corporations are using stock to compensate outside directors rather than retirement benefits amid growing shareholder demands for accountability, Towers Perrin said Wednesday.

The New York-based management consulting firm said 44 percent of 250 large corporations surveyed reported the use of defined benefit retirement plans for their outside directors, down sharply from 69 percent a year ago.
That percentage should keep falling over the next few years, as shareholder groups continue to criticise retirement plans, Towers Perrin said.
"More and more companies want to ensure that directors remain closely focused on shareholder issues," said Paula Todd, head of Towers Perrins' executive compensation research unit.
"To achieve this objective, companies need to set a substantial stock ownership target for directors and tie a significant portion of the director's pay package to the value of the company's stock."

Most companies that dropped retirement plans are now focusing on increasing the amount of stock their outside directors hold. Many firms converted directors' accrued benefit balances into deferred stock accounts that must be held as long as they remain on the board.
Most of these companies also restructured their pay packages to provide a larger proportion of the total package in stock, Towers Perrin said.

Stock ownership is also a priority at the companies surveyed, it said. Nine percent of them had stock ownership guidelines for their outside directors, and 31 percent made substantial initial or one-time stock grants in 1995, presumably to help jump-start ownership, Towers Perrin said.
Half of those one-time grants had an expected value of $72,000 or more, while one-quarter exceeded $130,000, it said.
Eight out of 10 companies now make annual or recurring stock compensation grants, mainly in the form of stock options, to directors, Towers Perrin said.

The cash portion of compensation packages has remained relatively stable over the last few years. In 1995, the median retainer for a director was $25,000, unchanged from the past several years, Towers Perrin said. The median meeting fee was steady at $1,000.
Half of all directors earn more than the median point, while half earn less.

Total cash compensation, including cash board retainer, meeting fees and cash retainers and fees for committee service was $44,000. Total annual compensation including stock was $64,000, and including retirement benefits was $71,000, Towers Perrin said.
